title: The Politics of the Bad Die: Why Advanced-Packaging Subsidies Should Buy Transparency, Not Just Capacity
artefact:
# The Politics of the Bad Die: Why Advanced-Packaging Subsidies Should Buy Transparency, Not Just Capacity

When governments subsidize semiconductor plants, they usually count tangible things: clean-room area, wafers started per month, tools installed, and jobs announced. That accounting made some sense when a high-value processor was largely identified with the wafer on which it was fabricated. It is increasingly misleading in an era of chiplets, high-bandwidth memory, silicon interposers, fan-out redistribution layers, and hybrid bonding. A modern accelerator can depend on logic fabricated at one site, memory stacked at another, an interposer or bridge made at a third, and final assembly and test performed at a fourth. The economically meaningful product emerges not from any one wafer but from the package.

This shift creates a political problem disguised as an engineering detail: who bears the cost when one component in an expensive package fails? The answer is determined by access to yield data, test coverage, interface rules, and contractual power. Dominant firms can demand known-good die, reserve scarce packaging lines, and push failure costs onto suppliers. Smaller chip designers, public research laboratories, and domestic manufacturers often cannot. If a government merely pays for additional packaging capacity, it may strengthen the firms already best positioned to control these terms.

The Meridian Republic, a fictional mid-sized industrial democracy, is considering 18 billion merins in support for advanced chip packaging. Its debate offers a useful model for other jurisdictions. Meridian should not condition aid primarily on the number of packages shipped or the nominal capacity of subsidized plants. It should use public money to create a **transparent failure regime**: auditable package-level yield reporting, fair access to qualification lines, limited interface escrow, and shared rules for allocating the cost of defective die and assembly failures. The objective is not to make proprietary packaging technology public. It is to prevent public subsidies from underwriting a private system in which the most powerful buyer alone can see, price, and survive failure.

## Packaging is where separate risks become one risk

Advanced packaging is sometimes described as a less glamorous companion to leading-edge fabrication. That description ignores both the technical difficulty and the economic leverage involved. In a conventional package containing one mature die, assembly loss may be tolerable because the component entering the line is relatively inexpensive. In a 2.5D accelerator, the package may combine a large compute chiplet, several input-output tiles, multiple stacks of high-bandwidth memory, and a wide interconnect structure. The package can become worthless if a single indispensable element is defective or if bonding, alignment, substrate warpage, thermal cycling, or redistribution-layer defects interrupt the completed system.

The arithmetic is severe even before assembly defects are considered. Suppose a design requires eight memory stacks, each with a 99.2 percent probability of passing incoming inspection, plus four logic chiplets at 98.5 percent each. If those probabilities are independent, the chance that every required component is good is roughly 88 percent. Add a hypothetical 95 percent package-assembly yield, and only about 84 percent of attempted units emerge as functioning packages. These are illustrative assumptions rather than measurements from a production line, but they expose the compounding effect. Improving a single component is not enough; the package integrates multiple yield distributions and makes their interaction commercially decisive.

The independence assumption is also optimistic in some circumstances. Components from the same wafer lot may share defects. Marginal die may pass a probe test but fail after bonding or under the thermal conditions of a complete system. A substrate variation can affect several connections at once. Conversely, better test insertion and redundancy can reduce the apparent compounding. The important point is not one universal yield figure. It is that the party possessing package-level data can distinguish among die defects, assembly defects, test escapes, and design incompatibilities. That knowledge determines who pays for scrap and who learns quickly enough to improve.

Yield data therefore functions as a form of market power. A large integrated buyer can correlate wafer lots, assembly tools, bonding recipes, thermal maps, and field returns. It can threaten to redirect volume if a supplier refuses liability. A small chiplet firm may receive only a pass-or-fail result and an invoice for lost package starts. A university spinout may never obtain enough line time to establish statistically meaningful failure patterns. The asymmetry is not merely unfair in an abstract sense. It can prevent technically sound entrants from surviving the qualification period in which failures are common and their causes are disputed.

## Capacity subsidies can entrench the bottleneck

Meridian’s current proposal would award grants according to installed tools, forecast throughput, domestic payroll, and the share of output reserved for nationally important customers. These criteria are understandable. They are also too easy to satisfy without changing the structure of access.

A subsidized operator could install hybrid-bonding equipment, announce thousands of package starts, and reserve the best process windows for two anchor customers. Less powerful users might be directed to short engineering runs with higher setup charges and weaker failure analysis. The operator could count every attempted package toward its public capacity commitment even if a large fraction were scrapped for reasons never disclosed to the customer. The state would have purchased machines, but not a usable market.

This is especially consequential because packaging capacity is not interchangeable. A nominal line for fan-out processing cannot automatically handle a large interposer assembly. Bond pitch, die size, thermal budget, mold behavior, substrate availability, test hardware, and the maturity of a particular process flow all matter. Even two lines using similar equipment may not offer equivalent yields. Counting package starts as though they were barrels of a standardized commodity conceals these differences.

Nor should Meridian assume that domestic location guarantees broad domestic benefit. A local packaging plant could remain operationally dependent on imported substrates, overseas memory stacks, proprietary test software, and a single foreign anchor customer. It might employ technicians and engineers, which is valuable, while still giving local chip designers no practical path onto the line. National flags do not dissolve bargaining power.

The political temptation is to ignore these complications because ribbon cuttings reward visible construction. Yield governance is harder to photograph. Yet it is precisely the less visible layer that determines whether a subsidized facility becomes shared industrial infrastructure or a publicly discounted extension of one company’s supply chain.

## A public bargain centered on failure transparency

Meridian should attach four conditions to grants above 200 million merins. The conditions would apply only to activity supported by public funds, not to every package made by a recipient.

First, recipients should maintain an **auditable yield ledger**. For each subsidized process family, the ledger would record aggregate incoming-die rejection, assembly loss, rework, final-test loss, and field-return categories. Customers would receive results for their own lots at greater detail, including agreed failure classifications and uncertainty ranges. The public would see only aggregated bands, protecting sensitive product information. An independent technical office could inspect raw records under confidentiality rules.

The ledger would not require a firm to reveal a bonding recipe or the layout of a customer’s die. Its purpose would be to separate questions that are too often bundled together: Did the die arrive defective? Did the assembly process damage it? Did the interface specification omit a relevant tolerance? Is the failure cause genuinely unknown? A category for unresolved failures is essential; otherwise operators would be pressured to assign blame prematurely. Repeatedly high unresolved rates would trigger review rather than an automatic penalty.

Second, subsidized plants should devote a modest share of qualified line time—perhaps 12 percent after the first production year—to **open qualification windows**. Eligible users would include small domestic designers, public laboratories, and firms developing components that can interoperate with more than one system vendor. Access would not be free. It would be offered at published, cost-based rates, with standardized rules for minimum lot size, cancellation, and failure analysis. A lottery or rotating queue could allocate oversubscribed windows, while emergency national needs would require a publicly documented exception.

Third, grant recipients should place a narrowly defined set of **interface and test artefacts in escrow**. These might include electrical tolerance envelopes, mechanical keep-out rules, thermal boundary assumptions, test-vector formats, and reference coupons needed to verify that a chiplet can enter the supported process. Escrow would be released to a replacement operator if a subsidized line closed, refused its access obligation, or became unavailable during a declared supply emergency. The underlying die design, proprietary process recipe, and customer netlist would remain protected.

Fourth, contracts should establish a default **failure-cost ladder**. If incoming inspection identifies a defective die, the die supplier bears the direct loss. If assembly is shown to have caused damage, the packaging operator bears it. If both parties accepted an interface outside the qualified envelope, they share the loss according to a pre-agreed formula. Where the cause remains unknown after specified analysis, liability is divided rather than automatically imposed on the weaker party. Sophisticated parties could negotiate different terms with private money, but subsidized qualification runs would begin from this public default.

These rules would turn yield from an opaque verdict into a jointly examinable production result. They would also give Meridian a more meaningful definition of capacity. A line that starts many packages but produces low, unexplained yield would no longer look equivalent to a line that supports stable output and learning across several customers.

## Why transparency is not the same as compulsory openness

Opponents will argue that interface escrow and yield auditing amount to forced disclosure. That objection has force if the policy is drafted carelessly. Advanced packaging contains valuable intellectual property in bonding sequences, materials, test methods, thermal structures, and co-design practices. Requiring publication of all process details would deter investment and could make sensitive systems easier to imitate or disrupt.

But there is a difference between revealing how a process achieves its tolerances and stating what tolerances an entering component must meet. A railway operator can specify axle loads without surrendering the design of its signaling system. Likewise, a packaging operator can disclose an electrical and mechanical acceptance envelope without publishing every step that makes the process work. The boundary will sometimes be disputed, but the existence of borderline cases is not a reason to leave every term under unilateral control.

Meridian should therefore create three disclosure tiers. Customer-specific lot data would be available to the customer and auditor. Process-family performance bands would be available to qualified potential users under nondisclosure terms. Only broad metrics—such as the proportion of subsidized line time used, median qualification delay, and unresolved-failure rate—would be public. Criminal penalties for intentional theft would remain, while ordinary classification disagreements would go to a specialist tribunal rather than becoming accusations of espionage.

Security requires further qualification. Packages used in defense, critical communications, or identity systems may need compartmented records and restricted access. Yet a blanket security exemption would swallow the policy. Meridian should exempt a product only when a designated authority identifies a specific risk, and the exemption should expire unless renewed. Even restricted lines should report aggregate utilization and yield to cleared auditors.

## The distributional stakes extend beyond chip companies

A failure-centered subsidy policy may sound remote from ordinary political concerns. It is not. Public spending on chip infrastructure competes with housing, transport, education, and climate adaptation. If Meridian directs 18 billion merins to packaging plants, citizens are entitled to more than assurances that the industry is strategically important. They should know whether the investment creates durable capabilities or merely lowers costs for firms that would retain the most valuable knowledge elsewhere.

The design of access rules also affects which regions can participate. Leading-edge wafer fabrication tends to concentrate around enormous capital pools and established supplier clusters. Packaging offers a somewhat broader range of entry points: substrate inspection, thermal characterization, reliability testing, failure analysis, equipment maintenance, and lower-volume integration. These activities still demand substantial skill and capital, but they do not all require a leading-edge wafer fab. Open qualification windows could connect technical institutes in Meridian’s inland manufacturing cities to nationally funded lines on the coast.

That promise should not be exaggerated. A reserved window cannot compensate for a weak design, a missing substrate supplier, or an underfunded laboratory. Small firms may struggle to prepare documentation or purchase enough known-good die. Meridian should pair access with shared test-vehicle programs and training grants, but it should avoid calling every workshop an innovation hub. The measure of inclusion is whether new users complete qualification and reach repeat production, not how many applicants attend an orientation session.

Workers also bear package-level risk. When a line misses yield targets, managers may respond with unstable shifts, extensive overtime, or pressure to bypass process controls. Subsidy contracts should require recipients to report scheduled and actual working hours by job category, protect technicians who stop a run over documented contamination or safety concerns, and fund portable credentials in metrology, bonding, and failure analysis. These provisions are not substitutes for collective bargaining, but they reduce the chance that commercial uncertainty will be transferred downward as arbitrary scheduling and blame.

Municipalities face a parallel risk. Advanced packaging generally uses less water than a major wafer fab, but clean operations, cooling, plating, and waste treatment still impose infrastructure demands. Meridian should require site-specific utility plans and public disclosure of normal and drought-stage consumption bands. A city should not be pressured into subsidizing water and power upgrades based on headline capacity that the operator may never use. If actual demand exceeds the contracted band, the operator—not residential ratepayers—should finance the additional infrastructure unless the city approves a new bargain.

These labor and municipal conditions may seem appended to the central yield argument. In fact, they reflect the same principle: uncertainty should not be hidden and assigned to the party with the least information. A technician, a small chip designer, and a host city occupy very different positions, but each can be asked to absorb risks that a subsidized operator is better able to measure.

## A stylized comparison of subsidy choices

Consider two hypothetical bids for 3 billion merins. North Quay Integration proposes a high-volume line expected to attempt 600,000 complex packages annually, with 90 percent final yield once mature. It reserves nearly all output for two anchor customers and reports only shipments. Common Assembly Works proposes 420,000 attempts at an expected 87 percent yield. It offers detailed failure reporting, open qualification windows, and process support for six package configurations.

On a simple shipment count, North Quay appears superior: 540,000 good packages versus roughly 365,000. If national policy values only near-term output, it should win. But suppose one anchor customer leaves in year four and the line’s tooling and test flow are difficult for others to adopt. Common Assembly’s lower initial output may support a wider supplier base and make capacity easier to repurpose.

Meridian should not automatically select the more open bid. It should score three distinct values: reliable output, adaptability, and access. A possible grant formula could assign 50 percent to expected good packages adjusted for technical risk, 25 percent to demonstrated changeover and qualification capability, and 25 percent to access and reporting commitments. The exact weights are political choices, not engineering facts. They should be published before bids arrive so officials cannot invent criteria to favor a preferred applicant.

This framework still relies on forecasts supplied by bidders. Auditors cannot fully verify a process that has not yet been built, and firms may manipulate category definitions after production begins. Meridian could withhold 20 percent of each grant until three years of operating data are available, but delayed payment raises financing costs and may advantage larger firms. There is no mechanism that eliminates strategic behavior. The goal is a contract in which exaggeration is more detectable and less profitable than under a raw capacity target.

## The strongest objections

The first serious objection is speed. Packaging technologies and demand can change faster than a public rulebook. A detailed access mandate might lock subsidized operators into interfaces that become obsolete, while approval procedures delay urgent equipment purchases. Meridian should answer by defining obligations around process families and measurable outcomes rather than named architectures. A recipient could replace one bonding method with another if it continued to provide the contracted level of qualification access and documented how existing users would migrate.

The second objection is that open windows could damage the economics of a line. High-volume packaging benefits from stable recipes, repeated products, and predictable materials. Frequent changeovers introduce contamination risks and consume engineering time. That is why a limited 12 percent allocation is preferable to a general common-carrier requirement. Rates should include genuine setup and engineering costs. The obligation is to offer a path, not to pretend that low-volume experimental work costs the same as a mature production run.

The third objection is geopolitical. Foreign suppliers might refuse to provide detailed die data to a Meridian-audited facility, and other governments could retaliate against access preferences for domestic firms. This risk is real. Meridian should permit firms from partner jurisdictions to use open windows on reciprocal terms and should develop common failure categories with those partners. Still, reciprocity may prove slow, and the proposed policy cannot guarantee access to high-bandwidth memory or advanced substrates controlled abroad. Transparent packaging governance is a resilience measure, not self-sufficiency.

The fourth objection concerns public competence. A subsidy office may lack engineers capable of evaluating hybrid-bonding yield or distinguishing a legitimate trade secret from an interface requirement. Meridian would need a professionally paid Packaging Accountability Bureau with rotating technical panels and strict conflict rules. Recruiting experts from industry risks regulatory capture; excluding them risks ignorance. Fixed-term appointments, disclosure of recent financial ties, and review by mixed panels would reduce but not resolve the tension.

Finally, dominant customers may simply decline the subsidy and build closed lines elsewhere. That outcome should not automatically be considered a policy failure. Public money is not owed to every strategically important company. However, if Meridian’s conditions are so costly that no credible operator applies, officials should revise them rather than celebrate purity while the country remains dependent. A five-year review should compare actual good-package output, customer diversity, qualification time, and fiscal cost against unsubsidized alternatives.

## What the public should purchase

Advanced packaging turns many separate components into one system, but it also turns separate commercial risks into a contest over blame. The firm that controls package-level information can decide whether a failed unit represents bad memory, weak bonding, an unrealistic interface, or an unexplained loss charged to someone else. Governments that subsidize equipment without addressing that power are not neutral. They finance the existing allocation of uncertainty.

Meridian should purchase more than nominal throughput. It should purchase the capacity to learn across firms, to qualify new entrants, to move production when a supplier fails, and to identify where publicly supported value is being lost. Auditable yield ledgers, limited open windows, interface escrow, and default failure-cost rules would not make packaging simple or fully competitive. They would make the consequences of failure more visible and negotiable.

The larger democratic principle is modest: when the public absorbs industrial risk, the public may demand institutions that prevent risk from being passed invisibly to weaker participants. In advanced packaging, that demand must reach below the factory roof and into test categories, interface envelopes, and qualification queues. The future of chip policy will not be decided only by who can fabricate the smallest transistor. It will also be decided by who owns the bad die—and who is allowed to know why it failed.
